--- toc-title: In this lesson --- # 11 `geopandas` GeoPandas is a Python library that extends the `pandas` library by adding support for geospatial data. In this lesson we will introduce the `geopandas` library to work with vector data. We will also make our first map. ## About the data Wild pigs (*Sus scrofa*) are a destructive invasive species in California, causing significant environmental and agricultural damage. Introduced to the region in the 1700s, they have since spread across the state, impacting native ecosystems through habitat destruction, soil disturbance due to their rooting behavior, and competition with native wildlife for food @finzel_wild_2015. This widespread damage has made managing wild pig populations a critical issue for conservation and agricultural communities in California. ![Wild pig in Santa Teresa Park, CA. [Photo by Don DeBold](https://www.flickr.com/photos/ddebold/52936296848)](/book/images/lesson-10/wild_pig.png){width="70%"} In this lesson we will use simplified point data about wild pig occurrence records in California from the [Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF)](https://www.gbif.org). GBIF is an international network and data platform that provides open access to biodiversity data from around the world. By aggregating data from multiple sources, including museums, research institutions, and citizen science initiatives like iNaturalist, GBIF enables scientists, policymakers, and the public to explore and analyze species distribution and environmental trends. The data we will use today has been simplified from the complete *Sus scrofa* occurrence data accessed through the GBIF website @gbiforg_user_occurrence_2023. This data is shared under a [Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 (CC BY-NC 4.0)](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/) license: we can use and share it as long as we credit the source and don't use it for commercial purposes. Each row in the data is one occurrence record. The column names were shortened to fit the 10-character limit of shapefile column names: | Column | Description | |--------|-------------| | `gbifID` | Unique identifier of the record in GBIF. The full record is at `https://www.gbif.org/occurrence/` followed by this ID. | | `species` | Scientific name of the species | | `state` | State where the record was made | | `individual` | Number of individuals recorded | | `day`, `month`, `year` | Date of the record | | `inst` | Code of the institution that provided the record, for example a museum or a citizen science platform | | `collection` | Code of the collection within that institution | | `catalogNum` | Identifier of the record in the institution's catalog | | `identified` | Person or institution who identified the species | | `geometry` | Location of the record | We will also use a shapefile with the boundary of the state of California, which has a single feature: the outline of the state. This boundary comes from the US Census Bureau's 2016 TIGER/Line shapefiles @us_census_bureau_tiger_2016 and was converted to a different CRS for this lesson. We will use it as a base layer for our maps, to see where the wild pig records are located within California. Both datasets are in the `gbif_sus_scrofa_california` and `ca_state_boundary` folders of the course's [shared data folder]({{< var shared-data-folder >}}). ## `geopandas` In this lesson we will introduce the `geopandas` @jordahl_geopandasgeopandas_2020 Python package. `geopandas` extends `pandas` to work with geospatial data. This is the main package we will be working with in the next few lessons. Let's start by importing the necessary packages and our data: ::: {#d0146ad7 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import os import geopandas as gpd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt ``` ::: ::: {#b325a864 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} fp = os.path.join('data','gbif_sus_scrofa_california','gbif_sus_scrofa_california.shp') pigs = gpd.read_file(fp) pigs.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=56} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-caution} ## One shapefile = multiple files Although the parameter for `geopandas.read_file()` is only the file with `.shp` extension, remember that we need to have at least the `.shx` and `.dbf` files in the same directory as the `.shp` to read in the data. ::: ## `GeoSeries` and `GeoDataFrame` The core data structure in GeoPandas is the `geopandas.GeoDataFrame`. We can think of it as a `pandas.DataFrame` with a dedicated geometry column that can perform spatial operations. The **geometry column** in a `geopandas.GeoDataFrame` holds the geometry (point, polygon, etc.) of each spatial feature. This geometry column is of type `geopandas.GeoSeries`. Columns in the `geopandas.GeoDataFrame` with attributes about the features are `pandas.Series` like in a regular `pandas.DataFrame`. ![Image adapted from [*Introduction to GeoPandas*](https://geopandas.org/en/stable/getting_started/introduction.html).](/book/images/lesson-10/geodataframe.png){width="70%"} #### Example First, notice that the rightmost column of the `pigs` geo-dataframe is a column named `geometry` whose values indicate points: ::: {#bb621dc2 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} pigs.head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=58} ```{=html}
gbifID species state individual day month year inst collection catalogNum identified geometry
0 899953814 Sus scrofa California NaN 22.0 3.0 2014.0 iNaturalist Observations 581956 edwardrooks POINT (-121.53812 37.08846)

2 896560733 Sus scrofa California NaN 20.0 12.0 1937.0 MVZ Hild MVZ:Hild:195 Museum of Vertebrate Zoology, University of Ca... POINT (-122.27063 37.87610)
``` ::: ::: As usual, we can check the type of our objects using the `type` Python function: ::: {#d8ab9a7d .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Check the data type of the pigs dataframe print(type(pigs)) # Check the data type of the geometry column print(type(pigs.geometry)) # Check the data type of the gbifID column print(type(pigs['gbifID'])) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ``` ::: ::: The data type of the geometry column is also reflected when we look at the data types of the values in each column: ::: {#13f5161b .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Check the data type of each column pigs.dtypes ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=60} ``` gbifID int64 species object state object individual float64 day float64 month float64 year float64 inst object collection object catalogNum object identified object geometry geometry dtype: object ``` ::: ::: We can also check the type of each element in the geometry column using the `geom_type` attribute of a `geopandas.GeoDataFrame`: ::: {#f81110fc .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} pigs.geom_type ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=61} ``` 0 Point 1 Point 2 Point 3 Point 4 Point ... 1041 Point 1042 Point 1043 Point 1044 Point 1045 Point Length: 1046, dtype: object ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## Check-in What is the geometry type of the single feature in the California state boundary? ::: ## CRS Two other important attributes of a `geopandas.GeoDataFrame` are its coordinate reference system (CRS) and its extent. We can think of the **coordinate reference system (CRS)** as the instructions to locate each spatial feature of our data frame on the surface of the Earth. We access the CRS of a `geopandas.GeoDataFrame` using the `crs` attribute: ::: {#0757fad5 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Access the CRS of the GeoDataFrame pigs.crs ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=62} ``` Name: WGS 84 Axis Info [ellipsoidal]: - Lat[north]: Geodetic latitude (degree) - Lon[east]: Geodetic longitude (degree) Area of Use: - name: World. - bounds: (-180.0, -90.0, 180.0, 90.0) Datum: World Geodetic System 1984 ensemble - Ellipsoid: WGS 84 - Prime Meridian: Greenwich ``` ::: ::: The CRS for our data is the World Geodetic System 1984 (WGS84), represented by the code EPSG:4326. It uses latitude and longitude in degrees to represent places on Earth. This is a very popular CRS: it is used by GPS and Google Earth, and web-based mapping tools like Google Maps and OpenStreetMap store their coordinates in it. We can obtain more information about our CRS by accessing other attributes: ::: {#d836c145 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Examine CRS details print('Ellipsoid: ', pigs.crs.ellipsoid) print('Datum: ', pigs.crs.datum) print('Is geographic?: ', pigs.crs.is_geographic) print('Is projected?: ', pigs.crs.is_projected) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Ellipsoid: WGS 84 Datum: World Geodetic System 1984 ensemble Is geographic?: True Is projected?: False ``` ::: ::: ## Extent The **extent** of the geo-dataframe is the bounding box covering *all* the spatial features in our geo-dataframe. This is formed by finding the points that are furthest west, east, south, and north. ![Spatial extent of different vector data. Image adapted from: National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON)](/book/images/lesson-10/spatial-extent-annotated.png){width="80%"} We access the extent of a `geopandas.GeoDataFrame` using the `total_bounds` attribute: ::: {#56ea260d .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Obtain the geographic extent of the geo-dataframe pigs.total_bounds ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=64} ``` array([-124.29448 , 32.593433, -115.4356 , 40.934296]) ``` ::: ::: These four numbers represent the `minx`, `miny`, `maxx`, `maxy` values for the bounds of the entire geo-dataframe. Notice that the $x$ values are longitudes and the $y$ values are latitudes: even though the CRS information above lists latitude first, `geopandas` follows the convention ($x$, $y$) = (longitude, latitude). ::: {.callout-tip} ## Check-in Print the CRS and extent of the California state boundary. ::: ## `explore()` To explore our data interactively, we can use the `explore()` method. This creates an interactive map where we can zoom in and out, move around, and hover over each feature to see its attributes: ::: {#e1fadc82 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} pigs.explore() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=66} ``````````{=html}

Describe a situation where these records would still be relevant to an analysis. ::: ## Data wrangling GeoPandas is conveniently built on top of `pandas`, so we may use everything we have learned about data selection, wrangling, and modification for a `pandas.DataFrame` to wrangle `geopandas.GeoDataFrame`s. #### Example We only want to use recent data for wild pig observations. Before selecting the data, let's look at which years it covers. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Check-in Before running the next cell, write down your prediction: when do you expect the earliest wild pig record in our data to be? Think about when wild pigs arrived in California and who could have recorded them back then. ::: ::: {#0e2c9b44 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Examine pig observations by year pigs['year'].value_counts().sort_index() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=67} ``` year 1818.0 31 1910.0 1 1925.0 1 1927.0 4 1929.0 3 ... 2019.0 101 2020.0 159 2021.0 164 2022.0 185 2023.0 98 Name: count, Length: 61, dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## Check-in 1. Does the earliest year match your prediction? Do you trust it? 2. Run `pigs[pigs['year'] == 1818]`. What do these records have in common? How much do you trust the year now, and where could you check it? ::: In this analysis, we will use data from 2020 onwards. We can use our usual data selection to subset it: ::: {#3476a3b4 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Select data from 2020 onwards pigs_recent = pigs[pigs['year'] >= 2020] # Check length of original dataframe print('Total number of observations: ' , len(pigs)) # Check length of new dataframe print('Number of observations since 2020: ' , len(pigs_recent)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Total number of observations: 1046 Number of observations since 2020: 606 ``` ::: ::: Notice that this selection also leaves out the records without a year, since a missing value is never greater than or equal to 2020. ## Visualizing our data ### `plot()` Similarly to a `pandas.DataFrame`, a `geopandas.GeoDataFrame` has a `plot()` method that we can call directly to create a quick, static view of our data. The geospatial information of the `geopandas.GeoDataFrame` will be used to create the axes of the plot. #### Example Let's take a quick look at our recent pigs data: ::: {#175259da .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} pigs_recent.plot() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lesson-10-geopandas-intro_files/figure-html/cell-16-output-1.png){width=368 height=411} ::: ::: ### Using `matplotlib` Going forward, we will make more complex visualizations where we add different layers to a map and customize it. To do this, we will use `matplotlib` via its `pyplot` interface for creating visualizations. You can review the `matplotlib` basics in this [previous lesson](/book/chapters/lesson-18-linear-regression/lesson-18-linear-regression.qmd). #### Example When using matplotlib, it can be useful to think of creating a plot as adding layers to an axes. In this case, the first layer that we want to add to our axes is the `pigs_recent` point data. We can plot our data using `matplotlib` like this: ::: {#a9c2f7ef .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Initialize empty figure and axes fig, ax = plt.subplots() # Add pigs point plot to our figure's axes pigs_recent.plot(ax=ax) # Display figure plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lesson-10-geopandas-intro_files/figure-html/cell-17-output-1.png){width=368 height=411} ::: ::: Then some simple customization for our pigs data could look like this: ::: {#4b7c8a17 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Initialize empty figure fig, ax = plt.subplots() # Add data to axes pigs_recent.plot(ax=ax, # Add plot to axes alpha=0.5, # Adjust transparency color='brown' # Update point color ) # Update axes ax.set_title('Reported "Sus scrofa" sightings in CA (2020-2023)') ax.set_xlabel('Longitude') ax.set_ylabel('Latitude') # Display figure plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lesson-10-geopandas-intro_files/figure-html/cell-18-output-1.png){width=423 height=449} ::: ::: ## Exercises ::: {.callout-tip} ## Exercise 1 1. Add the California state boundary to the plot so the boundary appears behind the points as below. Before plotting, check that both layers have the same CRS using `pigs_recent.crs == ca_boundary.crs`. Don't forget to customize your graph! 2. Write a short caption for your map describing the spatial distribution of observations. What patterns or clusters do you notice? ::: {#12ace038 .cell execution_count=18} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lesson-10-geopandas-intro_files/figure-html/cell-19-output-1.png){width=428 height=449} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## Exercise 2 A local news site publishes our final map with the headline *"Wild pigs concentrated around the Bay Area"*. Discuss with a partner: - Does our map support this headline? - Who produced the records in our map, and how might that shape where the points are? Perhaps explore the `inst` column. - Explain what our map can and cannot tell us about where wild pigs are in California. Then suggest a better headline. :::
